doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Nursery school rhythm sticks, home records and church music
summary: His love of rhythm began in a nursery school marching band; at home his father played records and took him to Tulsa jazz gigs and a church.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Oh that was when I was in junior high school probably and got my first Gretsch catalogue. But I think the real genesis of the attraction was at Mrs. Rumbal’s nursery school in Tulsa, Oklahoma. And we had a marching band. And I was assigned what they called back then rhythm sticks. They were red of course, and were serrated so you could also make sounds by rubbing them like that. And she also had me play cymbals. And I still have one of the cymbals, it’s a little tiny cymbal about that big with a big wooden knob so your little hand and hold on to it. And I just couldn’t wait ‘til we marched every day. We’d march around the school and I’d either be playing my cymbals or my rhythm sticks. And I think that’s where I first really got that sensation of playing rhythm and doing it with other people. So that’s really where it all started, and everything else just sort of came into place, my father playing ragtime piano, there being music constantly in the house. When we sat down to dinner he’d put a record on and we’d listen to it and talk about it. My mother as well. He would take me to — there were some great traditional

jazz players in Tulsa at the time. And he would take me to some of their gigs and I’d listen to that and then on a number of occasions we’d go to an African-American church and listen to the music there. And we all know the kind of joyous sounds that come out of that. So that really, really enticed me as well.
